topic: What if the Moon were made entirely of water ice?
scientific_scope_note: A same-size, same-orbit pure-ice Moon is a thought experiment. About 31% lunar mass and sixfold full-Moon brightness are estimates; the tide diagrams show simplified forcing, not predicted heights at individual coasts. Wildlife and deep-ocean responses vary, and vapor loss is slow and uncertain.

youtube_shorts.title: What if the Moon were made of ice?
youtube_shorts.description:
Imagine the Moon keeping its size and orbit but turning entirely to ice. Its full phase could shine about six times brighter, while its mass would fall to roughly one third. Follow the change from a moonlit coast to smaller tides, shrinking mudflats, altered animal nights, possible deep-ocean mixing changes, and ice slowly turning to vapor.

The tide visuals are simplified diagrams. Real tidal ranges depend on each coastline, and ecological effects are uncertain.

Science context: NASA Moon and icy-moon facts; NOAA tidal-force guidance; NASA Earth Observatory on deep-ocean tidal mixing.

instagram_reels.caption: What if the Moon were made of ice? It would light up full-Moon nights—but its weaker tidal pull would reshape the rhythm of coasts. Watch an ice Moon replace the familiar gray one, then follow the effects from shorebirds to the deep ocean. Tide heights and wildlife responses are illustrative and depend on place and species.

facebook_reels.title: What if the Moon were made of ice? Here’s what would change on Earth
facebook_reels.description: Same size. Same orbit. A very different Moon. This cinematic science scenario follows brighter moonlight, a weaker lunar tide, narrower feeding flats for shorebirds, and a possible change in deep-ocean mixing. Coastal tide heights vary locally; the ocean and wildlife scenes illustrate possible effects.

tiktok.caption: What if our Moon were solid ice? Brighter nights, a lighter Moon, and the Sun taking over the tides. The coastal changes are simplified—real shorelines respond differently.
